outcome: The conjecture as stated (an operadic/little-disks structure on the Hochschild cochain complex of an associative algebra) was already proved by multiple independent methods well before the January 2024 snapshot (Tamarkin 1998/2000; Kontsevich-Soibelman 2000; McClure-Smith 2002; Voronov 2000; Lurie's ∞-categorical version). No development in the 2024-01-26 to present window resolves, reopens, or meaningfully narrows the classical (algebra-level) statement; the one within-window paper found extends the underlying technique to a different class of objects (algebraic schemes, including singular ones) rather than changing anything about the bullet's own statement.

disputes.summary: Multiple independent proofs of the same conjecture were produced nearly simultaneously around 1998-2002 (Tamarkin; Kontsevich-Soibelman; McClure-Smith; Voronov), and secondary sources vary on which is credited as 'the first real proof'. This predates the window and does not affect the status classification, but is worth flagging since sources disagree on primacy.

summary: Deligne's conjecture on Hochschild cohomology (the operadic/little-disks structure on the Hochschild cochain complex of an associative algebra) was resolved well before the frozen Wikipedia revision, with several independent proofs from 1998-2002 (Tamarkin; Kontsevich-Soibelman; McClure-Smith; Voronov) and a further ∞-categorical version by Lurie. The Wikipedia article itself, current as of a July 2026 edit, still describes the conjecture as proved by these authors and records no post-2024 resolution claim, consistent with the list simply being stale on this entry. Searching specifically for the 2024-01-26-to-present window, I found one relevant preprint: Sonja Farr, 'E2-algebra structures on the derived center of an algebraic scheme' (arXiv:2506.14069, submitted June 16, 2025), which recovers a canonical solution to Deligne's conjecture on Hochschild cochains 'in the affine and global cases, even for singular schemes' via an infinity-operadic-center argument. This is new work in the window, but it extends the conjecture's technique to a different class of objects (algebraic schemes, including singular ones) rather than resolving, reopening, or narrowing the classical statement about Hochschild cochains of an associative algebra that the Wikipedia bullet actually states -- per the scope rule (§3.1) this reads as a related/extended problem (different objects) rather than a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not change the status. I also found the 2023 Brav-Rozenblyum result establishing a 'cyclic Deligne conjecture' (arXiv:2305.10323) and its Calabi-Yau-structure applications; this is explicitly a variant with different hypotheses (cyclic structure, relative Calabi-Yau data) and predates the window regardless. No AI involvement was found in any of the sources checked: the Farr paper's acknowledgements thank only a human thesis advisor and an NSF grant, with no mention of AI, machine learning, or LLM tools anywhere in the text.
competing_reading: One could argue the Farr (2025) extension to singular schemes is a 'case' of the general conjectural picture in the broader sense that operadic Hochschild-cochain structures are being established in a strictly wider class of settings than the original algebra case, and that Wikipedia's own statement is loosely worded enough ('the operadic structure on Hochschild cochain complex') that it could be read as covering the geometric/scheme generalization too. Under that reading this would be `partial`, `ai_role` none, dated to 2025-06-16, direction `confirmed`. I judged this the weaker reading because the classical conjecture is specifically about associative algebras (per both the arXiv:9910126 solution and the Wikipedia article's own framing), and the scheme-level Deligne conjecture is treated in the literature (including by Iwanari 2020 and Brav-Rozenblyum) as its own strand of generalization rather than as an unresolved fragment of the original.
what_would_settle_it: Whether Wikipedia's own article or a mathematical survey treats the scheme-level/global Deligne conjecture as literally the same statement as the classical algebra-level one (in which case Farr's 2025 paper would count as a `partial` result in-window) or as a distinct, separately-posed generalization (as I read it, leaving the bullet `open_stale`).
